text: Heads, I riffle shuffle a sorted deck four times. Tails, a computer shuffles it perfectly. From the deck alone, how often could you tell which? Pick 50, 75, or 100%. Any simulation that mixes by random steps faces this question. Stopped too early, it still remembers where it started. The obvious check is the top card, the one you'd be dealt. Here's how often each card lands there, after four riffles. Almost flat. Only the old top card stands out, one time in 15. Judging by the top card, you'd be right 52% of the time. Four riffles look like plenty. A guesser who sees the whole deck does far better. The model cuts near the middle, then drops cards from each half in proportion to its size. Each half stays in order, so one riffle leaves two rising sequences. Runs of consecutive cards, reading left to right. Give each sequence its own level. The cut crosses each level once, so a riffle can at most split it in two. Three riffles. Eight. Four riffles. At most 16, this deck has 14. A perfect shuffle averages 26.5, and gives 16 or fewer once in 2 million decks. Call any deck with 16 or fewer riffled, and you'd be wrong about once in 4 million games. The top card can't see this. It lives in the order between cards. Bayer and Diaconis proved that in this model, decks with the same count are equally likely. So pile each deck onto its count. Blue is a perfect shuffle. Purple is 4 riffles.
